ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, connecting shoulder to elbow and serving as attachment for many muscles. Its anatomy determines patterns of fracture, neurovascular injury, and joint disease.

sections.p: The humerus spans from the glenoid fossa of the scapula to the trochlea and capitulum of the ulna and radius, forming the shoulder and elbow joints.
b: Proximal end: head, anatomical neck, greater/lesser tubercles
Distal end: capitulum, trochlea, medial/lateral epicondyles

sections.p: It is a cylindrical bone with a proximal epiphysis, a diaphysis, and a distal epiphysis; the medullary cavity contains red marrow in children and yellow marrow in adults.
b: Intertubercular groove holds the long head of biceps

sections.p: Anteriorly the brachial artery and median nerve lie in the bicipital groove; posteriorly the radial nerve runs in the spiral groove; laterally the deltoid muscle covers the proximal shaft.

The humeral head receives the anterior and posterior humeral circumflex arteries; the shaft is supplied by the profunda brachii and nutrient artery; distal epiphysis gets branches from the radial recurrent artery.
b: Compromise of circumflex arteries can cause avascular necrosis
Nutrient artery injury may impair healing

sections.p: Sensory and motor innervation to the bone itself is via periosteal branches of the radial, axillary, and musculocutaneous nerves.
Provides lever arm for shoulder abduction, flexion, and rotation; transmits forces from the hand to the trunk; houses marrow for hematopoiesis.
Fractures are common at the surgical neck, mid‑shaft, and distal metaphysis; they may be complicated by neurovascular injury, infection, or avascular necrosis.
b: Distal fracture → growth plate injury in children

t.b: Confirms fracture location, displacement, and joint involvement; if unavailable, use clinical alignment and neuro exam.
Defines complex intra‑articular patterns; essential for surgical planning when X‑ray unclear.
Detects occult fractures, marrow edema, and early avascular necrosis; useful if X‑ray normal but pain persists.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: anatomy of the proximal humerus, common nerve injury sites, and the concept of avascular necrosis after dislocation.
b: Remember radial groove runs posteriorly on the shaft
Axillary nerve lies inferior to the glenoid rim
Blood supply to head is tenuous after fracture

whenToSeekHelp: Absent radial pulse after humeral injury
Progressive neurological deficit (e.g., worsening wrist drop)

faq.q: Why is the humeral head prone to avascular necrosis?
faq.a: Its blood supply comes mainly from the circumflex arteries, which can be torn in dislocation or surgical‑neck fractures.

faq.q: What is the most common nerve injured with a mid‑shaft humeral fracture?
faq.a: The radial nerve, leading to wrist and finger extension weakness.

faq.q: How does a humeral fracture affect blood cell production?
faq.a: The proximal humerus contains red marrow; severe injury can transiently reduce marrow activity but usually recovers.
